A Finshots piece evaluates what happened ten years after the November 2016 demonetisation, when Prime Minister Narendra Modi announced that ₹500 and ₹1,000 notes would no longer be legal tender. The author recalls watching the news break during dinner at home, with people lining up outside ATMs to withdraw ₹400 in cash because only ₹100 notes were available then; UPI had existed for barely three months but was not yet used widely. Notes worth about ₹15 lakh crore vanished overnight, and most of India's cash-dependent informal sector suffered as almost everything ran on scarce cash.

The article then examines each stated objective against the data. On black money: 99.3% of banned notes came back, with only about ₹10,720 crore missing; before the ban it was expected that roughly ₹4-5 lakh crore held as untaxed cash would not return, but this did not happen because people earning untaxed income often park wealth in real estate, gold or shell companies rather than keeping all of it as cash. The RBI board had also warned beforehand that demonetisation was unlikely to significantly impact black money and counterfeit notes.

On fake currency: the author disputes the claim linking cash-in-circulation magnitude directly to corruption levels, using Japan (a cleaner economy) with about 20% cash-to-GDP versus India's around 12%, which has stayed fairly stable despite UPI growth because GDP also grew and many transactions—real estate, weddings, tips, rural small-shop payments—still occur in cash. NPCI is planning a fee for UPI transactions above ₹2,000, which could push some shops back to cash. On counterfeits: RBI data shows counterfeit notes detected per crore fell from 70 in FY16 to 13 in FY26 overall; but focusing on the higher-denomination ₹500 note (where counterfeiting is most common), fakes rose from 0.3 to 20 per crore between demonetisation and now, though this uses only new notes so FY17 was a poor baseline. Comparing old versus current ₹500 notes instead shows counterfeits fell from about 167 to 20 per crore—suggesting the anti-counterfeit goal was largely met; yet fakes were never a huge problem as they formed a tiny fraction of total notes, and demonetisation cost an estimated 1.5-2% loss in economic output while hurting the informal sector.

On widening the tax net (an objective added later): filing returns jumped partly because cash deposits could now be traced to PAN records, but GST arrived in 2017 along with wider TDS use; new filers earned about ₹2.7 lakh on average, barely above the ₹2.5 lakh threshold at the time, and direct tax collections rose only slightly from 5.53% of GDP in FY17 to 5.86% the following year before falling to 4.78% by FY21, then reaching a high of 6.73% in FY25 after the pandemic.

The final verdict: demonetisation nudged people toward digital payments and brought more into the tax-filing system—though the pandemic was also a powerful force pushing contactless payments, which leave trails that can eventually expand the tax base—but curbing black money clearly failed; this would require stricter law enforcement and measures to plug loopholes letting people park undisclosed income in other assets or buy property with cash. The author ends by noting that until then… (an incomplete sentence). A Ditto term insurance advertisement follows, addressed to breadwinners about financial security if they are not around.

The article is a Finshots piece; the source text is marked untrusted.
items.title: Demonetisation's decade: promises versus outcomes in India

items.summary: The article traces how air pollution in Delhi is pushing residents to leave the city, following two families. Mohammad Najir began collecting segregated door-to-door waste as a landfill worker at Bhalswa, one of three landfills in Delhi; over roughly two decades he watched that site grow into a mountain while his own health declined — first tuberculosis diagnosed in 2007 with eight months of medication, then asthma developing around 2019 whose symptoms worsened in the colder months. His wife Manoura Begum arranged for Najir to move to their ancestral village Madhubani in Bihar on the hope that cleaner air would help him; his breathing did improve somewhat but he could not work, and because Begum herself could not find employment there she returned alone to Delhi's Baprola area, leaving them separated. Around the same time, flower-seller Kalu moved out after his four-year-old son suffered frequent eye infections and a persistent cough that a doctor attributed to dust, pollution and vehicle emissions; unable to work in Rajasthan's Bhilwara district, he migrated about 1,700 km south to Bengaluru. These people are described as 'smog refugees' — those who relocate from polluted areas to cleaner ones for health reasons. In India most reported cases involve leaving Delhi, one of the world's most polluted capitals and among only between 50 and 100 'good' or 'satisfactory' air quality days per year over the last seven years. Such migrants are usually relatively privileged with financial means to move comfortably; more recently some lower-income households have made similar moves under considerable strain, though these cases remain far rarer. The costs for poorer families extend beyond money: Kalu had to remove his two older children from their government school in Delhi and has not yet enrolled them anywhere in Bengaluru because the nearest one is too distant. Occupational exposure compounds vulnerability — Begum and Najir worked with unsegregated wet-and-dry waste that released toxic fumes, especially in summer, alongside frequent garbage-site fires; doctors told Najir his tuberculosis and asthma were likely work-related to Delhi's pollution. A 2023 report by the Chintan Environmental Research and Action Group comparing 100 waste pickers, safai karamcharis and security guards with a control group found that 75% of workers had abnormal pulmonary function versus 45% in controls, 17% suffered severe lung diseases (none in controls), and 26% reported breathing difficulty. Dr Shiva Kant Misra of Shivani Hospital IVF in Kanpur, part of the Doctors for Clean Air movement, explained that carbon monoxide, ozone, dust and smoke producing PM 2.5 and PM 10 irritate lungs and can multiply symptoms, with women, older people and young children especially affected; a 2018 Agra study found traffic-related pollution raised respiratory morbidity in children, with asthmatic episodes 1.79 times more likely among those living near traffic — the same exposure Kalu's son faced while his parents sold flowers on footpaths all day. Leaving also carries recurring costs: Begum said families like hers must save at least two to three months of earnings before relocating and may face unemployment, as she did after an office job in Netaji Nagar closed; for Kalu the round trip between Bengaluru and Bhilwara now takes about three days each way versus one day from Delhi, so his family travels only around once every four months. The move has helped: Bengaluru recorded AQI between 65 and 90 across 2015 and 2025, and Kalu's son is healthier there; but for Najir most damage appears done — breathlessness reduced yet he remains dependent on medication. Experts note psychological tolls too: Arjun Kamdar of Cambridge University said the rich can whimsically escape pollution (for example to Shimla), whereas forced relocation rattle lower-income migrants' identities and social standing, since they left cities seeking better lives only to leave them again. For many sufferers, leaving is not even an option — Virender Kumar of the Waste Picker Welfare Foundation works with waste pickers near a polluting waste-to-energy plant at Ghazipur landfill where women have had premature deliveries; one study found high PM 2.5 during pregnancy linked to 13% premature births and 17% low birth weight, and Kumar has seen men with kidney and lung diseases — yet these workers, many from West Bengal and Assam without land back home, cannot envision earning or feeding themselves after returning, so staying is their only option; Begum similarly wonders where people would go and how long they can keep 'running' from the air.
items.title: Delhi's pollution is driving health-driven migration among waste collectors and street vendors — but escape remains out of reach for many

items.summary: Ahead of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, China Media Group (CMG) hosted an event titled "Asia-Pacific of One Heart: Creating the Future Together – A CMG Media Gathering" in Shenzhen, Guangdong Province, on Monday, November 16, 2026. The gathering convened 69 representatives from media organizations across 62 countries, alongside delegates from Chinese media, businesses, and cultural and artistic sectors for discussions on technological innovation and media cooperation. Qi Zhuquan, vice president of CMG, addressed the event, calling on Asia-Pacific media to promote openness and cooperation, document innovation and development, foster mutual learning among civilizations, strengthen public understanding of a shared future, and contribute to common prosperity. Chen Xiaowei, deputy head of the Publicity Department of the CPC Guangdong Provincial Committee and director of the Information Office of the Guangdong Provincial People's Government, noted that APEC economies account for about two-thirds of Guangdong's foreign trade and more than 80% of its foreign investment, underscoring the province's close economic ties with the region; he added that people-to-people exchanges are as important as trade links and invited media representatives to experience Guangdong's openness. Alonso Millán Zepeda, director general of Mexican public cultural television station Canal 22, spoke of longstanding Mexico-China friendship and his organization's cooperation with CMG, calling for closer collaboration in cultural content production, audiovisual program exchanges, and exchanges among young media professionals. Presentations were also given by John Liu, executive editor at Bloomberg LP; Andrey Popov, a correspondent with TASS in Shanghai; Dong Mingzhu, chairwoman of Gree Electric Appliances, who highlighted the company's experience in manufacturing, research and development, core technology breakthroughs, innovation, talent, and health; Dr. Hua Wenli, a scientific officer with the China Meteorological Administration's World Meteorological Centre Beijing office, who introduced MAZU, China's intelligent meteorological early-warning solution and its use across multiple countries to improve disaster preparedness and international cooperation; and hosts Liu Yue, CMG host Liu Xin, and China-Arab TV reporter Fang Haoming. The event featured cultural performances drawing on diverse international influences. A special program featuring the event is scheduled for release on November 17 on CMG's new media platforms, including CCTV News, CGTN, and Voice of the Greater Bay Area.
items.title: CMG Media Gathering Brings Asia-Pacific Voices Together in Shenzhen

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) reported that Cyclone Akvan, centred over the south and adjoining west-central Bay of Bengal at 11:30 pm on November 17, is expected to intensify into a 'severe' cyclonic storm by the morning of November 18. It will then move northwestwards and further strengthen into a 'very severe' cyclonic storm by the evening of November 19. IMD Director K Nagarathna said the impacts are most likely heavy to very heavy rainfall at a few places in coastal Andhra Pradesh, light to moderate rains over many areas, and extremely heavy rains at one or two locations; offshore and onshore activities must be reviewed based on further advisories. The storm is projected to cross the Andhra Pradesh and Yanam coasts between Nellore and Visakhapatnam on November 20 as a 'very severe' cyclonic storm with maximum sustained winds of 120-130 kmph and gusts reaching 145 kmph.

The Andhra Pradesh Meteorological Department issued an official statement noting the storm had moved north-northwestwards slowly at about 3 kmph over the previous six hours, remaining centred near latitude 12.3°N and longitude 85.6°E — roughly 590 km east of Chennai, 630 km northeast of Trincomalee in Sri Lanka, 650 km southeast of Machilipatnam, 650 km south-southeast of Visakhapatnam, and 780 km south of Gopalpur in Odisha. The department said the storm was very likely to continue moving north-northwestwards slowly and intensify into a severe cyclonic storm over the west-central Bay of Bengal by Tuesday evening before strengthening further.

Odisha has shifted its focus toward landslide risk as Akvan approaches, even though landfall is expected in neighbouring Andhra Pradesh. District Magistrate Ashutosh Kulkarni said Rayagada district — located along the Odisha–Andhra border and issued yellow and orange warnings for November 18, 19, and 20 due to forecast heavy rainfall — has had around 55 landslide-prone villages identified for pre-emptive evacuation. Disaster Management Minister Suresh Pujari said landslides have become Odisha's major challenge; of the 11 deaths from last month's cyclone Arnab, 10 were caused by landslides. The state aims to shift over 2 lakh people (more than 200,000) from vulnerable foothill and hilltop areas across southern Odisha, with final numbers depending on conditions.

Preparedness measures include the Special Relief Commissioner's office directing the Odisha Remote Sensing Application Centre to supply satellite imagery and GIS-based maps of landslide-prone villages and road stretches in six highly vulnerable districts — Ganjam, Gajapati, Rayagada, Kandhamal, Malkangiri, and Koraput. The SRC also asked the Electronics and Information Technology Department to assess vulnerable telecom networks and deploy Cell-on-Wheels mobile units in advance in likely-affected districts.
items.title: Cyclone Akvan set to intensify into a very severe storm before Andhra landfall on November 20; Odisha braces for landslides and mass evacuation

Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant, in consultation with the four most senior judges—justices Vikram Nath, BV Nagarathna, MM Sundresh and PS Narasimha—shifted at least two matters away from a bench headed by justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah after those benches expanded individual disputes into nationwide public interest litigations (PILs). The move follows a full court meeting around four weeks ago in which the CJI stated that judges must adjudicate strictly within their assigned rosters to preserve orderly case allocation, judicial discipline and public confidence. According to people aware of the matter, Amanullah's roster does not include PILs; if his bench believed a matter required PIL treatment it should have referred it to the CJI through the court registry rather than assume jurisdiction.

The first case, Ayesha Jain Vs Amity University Noida, arose from a student's grievance over alleged harassment and loss of an academic year after she legally changed her name. The bench expanded proceedings into a nationwide examination of private university establishment, funding and regulation, issuing directions to the Centre, states and regulatory authorities. Regularly heard by justices Amanullah and NV Anjaria, it has now been assigned to a three-judge bench headed by justice Nath with justices R Mahadevan and Aparesh Kumar Singh as members, scheduled for November 19.

The second case, Loganathan vs State of Tamil Nadu, concerns unauthorised constructions and commercial misuse of residential properties. It began on March 25 after the court noted an individual Chennai case involving a one-and-a-half-storey building without an approved plan, then expanded to seek responses from states and municipal authorities in major cities including Delhi. Senior advocate Ajit Kumar Sinha was appointed amicus curiae with advocate Govind Jee assisting him; it is now expected before a bench headed by justice Nagarathna on November 23.

The decision draws on established jurisprudence affirming the CJI as master of the roster: Campaign for Judicial Accountability and Reforms (2017), which held that neither two- nor three-judge benches can allocate matters to themselves or dictate bench composition, and no judge may take up a matter unallocated by the CJI; State of Rajasthan Vs Prakash Chand (1997); Jasbir Singh Vs State of Punjab (2006), emphasising judicial discipline requires seeking appropriate orders from the chief justice rather than assuming jurisdiction; and Kishore Samrite Vs State of UP (2012), cautioning strict scrutiny when public interest is invoked. HT sought comments from justice Amanullah but received no response by press time.
items.title: CJI Surya Kant pulls two PIL cases from Justice Ahsanuddin Amanullah over roster violations

items.summary: Electric power tool brand Greenworks is expanding its battery-forward lineup by launching OPTIMUS, an all-new go-anywhere electric side-by-side utility vehicle (SxS). First shown at Equip Exposition 2026 in Kentucky last month, the redesigned UTV is described as the biggest and newest addition to the company's commercial ecosystem. Greenworks claims it integrates its purpose-built equipment and power platforms for professional property maintenance customers. Yin Chen, CEO of Greenworks, says OPTIMUS extends the brand's vision of pushing battery power beyond industry expectations, covering everything from maintained-property equipment to utility vehicles and charging systems. The vehicle is built around a 400V high-voltage electrical platform that mates two compact electric motors combining for 110 equivalent hp. Those motors draw on a 19 kWh lithium-ion battery pack with enough efficiency to reach a 40 MPH top speed and cover up to 68 miles of range under typical operating conditions. For hauling, OPTIMUS offers buyers a 2,500 lb towing capacity and 1,300 lb payload capacity along with 11 full inches of ground clearance and a 6,000 lb electric winch. Independent suspension, oversized all-terrain tires, torque vectoring differentials, and multiple terrain modes round out the spec sheet for demanding off-road applications. The article also references related items: Club Car Urban as an electric pickup in US; John Deere's updated Gator GX and GX Crew electric UTVs for 2026; CFMoto U6 electric side-by-side UTV; plus a promotional EnergySage solar installer service offering savings of 20-30% compared to going it alone. The article notes the '100 equivalent' hp figure is marked with an uncertainty indicator, and that Greenworks uses '?' notation around some specs in its own text.
items.title: Greenworks launches OPTIMUS electric UTV with over 100 equivalent hp and 68-mile range

Rhys Roberts, president of the Australia-China Business Council (ACBC), discusses China's importance as a trading partner for both Australia and the wider Asia-Pacific region. This interview frames China's market as central to business prospects for companies operating throughout the Asia-Pacific region during this APEC gathering in 2025. items.title: ACBC President: China Remains Key to Asia-Pacific Trade

items.summary: This piece opens an exploration of Shenzhen's transformation from a small fishing village into one of China's leading innovation centers in just over four decades. Bert Hofman, former World Bank country director for China, Mongolia and Korea, set out to understand how the city reinvents itself continually rather than simply growing. The framing emphasizes that what is striking about Shenzhen is not only how far it has come but how it keeps moving beyond its past to forge new paths. According to this account, Shenzhen's identity has shifted repeatedly: from being known as the 'world's factory' to becoming the 'Silicon Valley of hardware,' and now positioning itself as a hub for innovation and R&D. The article poses two central questions—how a small fishing village became one of China's leading innovation centers in just over four decades, and what has driven this remarkable transformation—and sets out to answer them by examining the city's history, industries, and the choices made by the people who have shaped its journey. This is part 1 of a series; no specific figures, dates, policies, or mechanisms are yet detailed beyond these framing observations about Shenzhen's reinvention across four decades.
items.title: Shenzhen: The Making of a Miracle (Part 1)

items.summary: America's largest weapons manufacturers face a January 1 Pentagon deadline requiring them to prove their magnets are free of Chinese rare earths, even though dysprosium and terbium—the two heavy rare earths used to keep powerful magnets working under extreme temperatures in fighter aircraft, missiles, and other advanced military equipment—are nearly entirely controlled by Beijing. China controls close to 100% of the processing for these metals. To address this dependency, Washington has proposed making 200 acres of a 43,000-acre Army depot in Utah available for REalloys (NASDAQ: ALOY) to build a heavy rare earth processing plant under a lease that could last up to 75 years. On November 3, REalloys and the U.S. Army signed a non-binding term sheet at Tooele Army Depot; REalloys would finance, construct, and operate the facility while the Army retains first opportunity to purchase its dysprosium and terbium production. The timing aligns with China's pause on expanded rare earth export controls, which Beijing extended two months to January 10, 2027—nine days after the Pentagon ban takes effect. Defense contractors have requested more time but Washington has kept the deadline in place. REalloys holds an advantage through its developing North American supply chain that converts rare earth oxides into metals; it is working with the Saskatchewan Research Council on what they describe as North America's first fully integrated commercial rare earth processing and metallization operation, while retired four-star General Jack Keane, a board member, warned China has made clear it is prepared to use this dependence as leverage. The Army lease would give REalloys long-term industrial presence on an American military installation with the Pentagon seeking first access; Waksman told Fox Business that the structure lets the Army expand the critical minerals industrial base without putting taxpayer dollars at risk, and CEO Lipi Sternheim said it puts part of the rare earth supply chain under military oversight. Keane called the term sheet 'an important step toward bringing heavy rare earth processing onto a U.S. defense installation.' The arrangement still requires REalloys and the Army to complete environmental review, permitting, and requirements before signing the final lease; the term sheet provides for a 50-year lease with a 25-year extension option, with REalloys paying fair-market rent plus participation rent once commercial operations begin. On processing capacity, magnet makers buy dysprosium and terbium as metal rather than oxide, and China ran nearly 100% of global heavy rare earth metallization until recently; outside China only a handful of plants make these metals—Less Common Metals in the U.K., the Korean Metals Plant at Ochang (which has made initial sales), and REalloys' Euclid, Ohio operation as the only North American heavy rare earth metallization capability. REalloys is scaling its $40 million plant built at SRC in Saskatoon before moving to Ohio; it will produce about 30 tonnes of dysprosium metal and 15 tonnes of terbium metal a year, with a provisional patent on a hydrofluoric acid-free fluorination process that could reduce capex, opex, and improve sustainability. Chairman Stephen duMont called the plant 'a critical link that's never existed at scale in the West,' while REalloys told Oilprice.com that dysprosium and terbium metals represent a major bottleneck for advanced magnet manufacturing. Within its integrated supply chain, SRC's CEO calls the partnership 'the Western hemisphere's first end-to-end rare earth metal capability.' REalloys' Euclid subsidiary Terves is developing engineering design for a 300-ton-a-year samarium and gadolinium metal plant under a Defense Logistics Agency contract awarded in March. REalloys holds rights to about 80% of SRC's expanded output—525 tonnes of NdPr metal, 30 tonnes of dysprosium oxide, and 15 tonnes of terbium oxide a year—and targets first NdPr metal from SRC in Q1 2027 with the dysprosium and terbium metallization plant commissioning in Q1 2028. On feedstock, REalloys locked in a 15-year offtake for 15% of Phase 1 production from Critical Metals' Tanbreez project in Greenland; it also signed non-binding agreements in Montana and Wyoming plus an Appalachian material memorandum of understanding. The company raised about $100 million in June and held $122.4 million in cash at quarter-end, saying its cash covers the Saskatchewan and heavy metallization projects through commissioning. Critical Metals Corp. (NASDAQ: CRML), which closed its merger with European Lithium on November 5 to own all of Greenland's Tanbreez project up from 42% at year start, reported about $264.5 million in cash after the merger and plans a definitive feasibility study by Q4 2027; first ore is not expected until late 2028 to early 2029, so Tanbreez feedstock remains a story for after the January deadline. Elsewhere, MP Materials (NYSE: MP) said on November 5 it completed General Motors' magnet qualification at its Independence plant in Fort Worth, Texas, with saleable deliveries and revenue starting Q4; that segment brought $18.6 million last quarter against $147.7 million total revenue, down 15% from a year earlier partly due to the start-up of magnet production there. In Oklahoma, USA Rare Earth (NASDAQ: USAR) made its first commercial magnet sale in September shipping sintered block magnets from Stillwater; Q3 revenue was only $3.0 million though it ended September with about $1.2 billion in cash and restricted cash after closing on Serra Verde with shipments beginning October and first sales recorded November. Further out, NioCorp Developments (NASDAQ: NB) is building the Elk Creek mine in southeast Nebraska to produce dysprosium oxide and terbium oxide alongside niobium and scandium; The U.S. Export-Import Bank said in October it still targets debt covering about 65% of roughly $1.85 billion in upfront costs subject to due diligence, and NioCorp signed a non-binding memorandum with Lockheed Martin for up to 15 tonnes a year of scandium oxide. Lockheed, RTX, General Dynamics, and Northrop now must hand the Pentagon a paper trail for every magnet installed—almost every dysprosium and terbium trail leading to China—with the White House order requiring them to trace 'all components, parts, equipment, software, and materials' back to raw-material origins; REalloys is building a trail that never touches China via Greenland feedstock from Tanbreez, separated oxide from Saskatchewan, metal from Euclid, and 200 acres on an Army base in Utah. This publication contains forward-looking statements involving risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ due to changing governmental laws and policies among other factors; neither the author nor Oilprice.com was paid for this communication concerning REalloys (NASDAQ: ALOY), though its owner holds shares or options of the featured company, creating a stated conflict requiring independent due diligence.
items.title: Pentagon Deadline Drives REalloys Rare Earth Magnet Push in Utah

items.summary: SolarEdge Technologies has unveiled its new Duo Power Optimizer, a U.S.-manufactured solution aimed at simplifying commercial and industrial (C&I) solar installations without sacrificing system performance. Announced November 16 ahead of RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, the product introduces a 2:1 architecture that allows one optimizer to connect two solar modules, cutting the number of power optimizers by 50% compared with traditional one-to-one designs while retaining independent maximum power point tracking (MPPT) for each module. For developers, EPCs and installers managing large-scale rooftop and distributed generation projects, this reduction targets fewer components to purchase, wire and install, along with streamlined balance-of-system requirements and reduced installation labor. The Duo addresses the limitation of conventional string inverter systems, where an underperforming module can affect the output of an entire string; by allowing each module to operate independently, it limits the impact of shading, degradation or performance differences between panels. Each optimizer features two input pairs: a shorter connection for the nearest module and a pre-extended connection for the adjacent module, reducing excess wiring and eliminating field-made jumpers. The configuration also accommodates modules with different orientations, making it relevant for east-west and dual-tilt racking applications. On safety, SolarEdge extends its Sense Connect technology to the optimizer's input and output connectors to monitor connector temperatures and identify developing issues before they escalate into overheating or electrical arcs. It introduces an industry-first approach to arc fault detection in which every optimizer acts as an individual arc sensor rather than relying exclusively on detection at the inverter, distributing monitoring throughout the array so faults can be identified closer to their source. SolarEdge says this provides coverage across strings with up to 3,280 feet of total cable length between the inverter and optimizer, potentially improving troubleshooting and maintenance efficiency. Manufactured at SolarEdge's Florida facility, the Duo is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements; its domestic-content eligibility levels are consistent with those of previous U.S.-manufactured power optimizers, subject to applicable tax guidance and project-specific requirements. For SolarEdge, the product combines installation efficiency, system-level safety, and domestic manufacturing into a single effort that does not fundamentally change the value proposition of module-level optimization but instead makes it more economical and easier to deploy at scale. The company will showcase the Duo Power Optimizer at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.
items.title: SolarEdge Unveils U.S.-Made Duo Power Optimizer for C&I Solar

items.summary: A court in The Hague on Tuesday convicted former Kosovo President Hashim Thaci of obstructing justice and attempting to influence witnesses during his war crimes trial, sentencing him to 17 months in prison. This term will be added to his existing 25-year sentence for war crimes handed down by the same court, the Kosovo Specialist Chambers, on September 16. According to the indictment of the Specialist Prosecutor's Office, Thaci had provided visitors at the detention facility with confidential information about witnesses and instructed them on how to influence their testimony. Three other men were also convicted: former head of the Kosovo Intelligence Agency Bashkim Smakaj, former Minister of Justice Hajredin Kuci, and Fadil Fazliu. Thaci was the former political leader of the Kosovo Liberation Army (KLA) during the 1998-1999 Kosovo War and is viewed by many in his home country as a hero; his September war crimes conviction was greeted with anger and dismay, and he has vowed to appeal it. His two convictions touch deep sensitivities in Kosovo society, renewing attention to the war that ended 27 years ago, the role of its former leaders, and ongoing debates over justice—individual versus collective responsibility for the KLA's campaign—and trust in judicial institutions. The government responded swiftly with a Tuesday statement asserting that "Justice must not only be done, but must also be fair, transparent, and credible." The Kosovo Specialist Chambers was established in 2015 by the parliament of Kosovo at the instigation of the European Union and the United States to investigate serious crimes allegedly committed by KLA members during and after the war; for security reasons including witness intimidation concerns, it is located in The Hague. After the September first-instance convictions, state authorities set up a working group chaired by Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca with parliament members to draft an appeal strategy. Prime Minister Albin Kurti stated that "the government is working to secure a correction at the appeals level before the Specialist Chambers," describing the judgment as unjust both legally and morally. Separately, Kosovo's parliament is considering amendments expected to be adopted, which would narrow the court's mandate by limiting its jurisdiction time period, capping maximum prison sentences at 15 years, allowing sentences to be served in Kosovo, and introducing presidential pardons for persons convicted by final decisions. Political analyst Artan Muhaxheri warned that from an international perspective this initiative "could even be interpreted as an attempt to interfere in the judicial process," stressing it must not conflict with Kosovo's obligations toward the European Union. Ehat Miftaraj of the Kosovo Law Institute noted that although the chambers were established by Kosovo itself, the process has created an impression that judges and prosecutors treated both the accused and Kosovo with distrust and a condescending approach; he affirmed citizens have the right to criticize judicial decisions but distinguished legal criticism from attempts to delegitimize courts. The article notes there is "room for criticism of both sides" regarding these reactions and objections, which are also judged in the historical and emotional context of the war.
items.title: Thaci's second conviction reignites Kosovo justice debate

The government has endorsed plans by former minister Alan Milburn for sweeping welfare reforms aimed at preventing a "generation" of young people from being lost to life on benefits. Milburn proposes spending billions on tailored support for under-25s not in employment, education or training (Neets), part-funded by cuts to some benefits. He claims his plan—which also includes tax breaks for firms and major education reforms—will get 440,000 young people into jobs by 2036.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he endorsed the "principles" of the Milburn review and was confident he could persuade Labour MPs to back legislation. Telling Sky News he would set out a full response next month—after receiving a separate report into Personal Independence Payments (Pips) by Social Security Minister Sir Stephen Timms—he described it as an unprecedented whole-government approach, saying "I have never in my years in politics seen a wholesale, whole government approach to supporting the next generation." The government has made Milburn head of a new youth opportunities unit to deliver on his recommendations.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said her party agreed with Milburn's "diagnosis" but claimed Labour had worsened conditions for young people by increasing employers' National Insurance contributions and the youth minimum wage. Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden, flanked by Burnham and Chancellor John Healey in Commons, rejected claims that young people were "snowflakes and shirkers," arguing welfare should be judged "not just by a snapshot of people's monthly incomes" but "by the story of people's lives." The government plans to publish draft proposals on welfare reform early next year.

In his 250-page report, Milburn proposes an entirely new benefits system for under-25s ending health-top-ups of Universal Credit and Personal Independence Payments (Pip), replacing them with a youth allowance at the basic rate. He also calls for reduced employers' National Insurance costs for 21-to-24-year-olds starting in retail and hospitality, expanded post-18 college places with a legal right to work or training, and a new locally-led Youth Opportunity Service giving each young person a named advisor. The report estimates spending around £5.8bn by 2036-37 on extra mental health and employment support, urging an initial £500m "kickstart" next year from reprioritising existing spending.

Milburn said his plans are not about saving money—overall savings would only emerge in 2036/27, when the government would claw back £200m. By then it assumes the share of 16-to-24-year-olds that are Neet will fall from 13%—one of the highest in Europe—to 5%, the lowest UK figure since records began.

The report has no specific blueprint for Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland, where education and skills are devolved. Milburn said the UK and devolved governments should agree common definitions and outcomes; Scotland's Education Secretary Màiri McAllan noted many recommended reforms were already in place there, while Welsh government stood ready to collaborate.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage called it "too little and too slow," Lib Dem treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper urged backing high street firms and scrapping the jobs tax, and Green Party leader Zack Polanski dismissed the proposals as a "flimsy sticking plaster" that would slash support for disabled young people while subsidising corporations. There are few signs Burnham will face the backlash his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer encountered over planned £5bn welfare cuts last year.
items.title: Government backs Milburn welfare reforms to prevent 'lost generation' of young people on benefits

Few cinematic choices are more subjective than ranking who played the best or worst James Bond, though such debates remain contested except in obvious cases. By official canon there have been seven actors in the role; an eighth, David Niven, appeared in Casino Royale (1967), a film made outside Eon Productions' umbrella and Ian Fleming's screen rights. The first actor to bring Bond to screen was American Barry Nelson in the 47-minute television adaptation of Casino Royale (1954), broadcast as part of CBS's Climax! series, though this is treated separately from the canonized list.

Summarizing time's judgment on each incarnation: George Lazenby received special kindness for his lone outing; Sean Connery remains the purists' Bond and created the character so completely that Fleming altered details in some later novels to match him; Roger Moore was the campiest, with a pop-era charm but lacking depth and gravitas; Timothy Dalton is favored by those who prefer the Bond closest to Ian Fleming's original creation; Pierce Brosnan got the role late in his career; and Daniel Craig's standing grew over time through films conceived almost as a self-contained series.

George Lazenby, ranked sixth, was the only actor from outside the British Isles (the United Kingdom and Ireland) to play 007 in canon. The Australian took on the role at 29, the youngest of all, but appeared in only one film, On Her Majesty's Secret Service, after signing a seven-picture deal; midway through production he announced he would make just that film amid his own doubts and pressure from his agent.

Pierce Brosnan, ranked fifth, was tied to Remington Steele when first offered the role. By the time he freed himself, he was a decade late for the double-0 designation, though GoldenEye (1995) gave him a strong start; some films like Die Another Day arguably went too far.

Roger Moore, ranked fourth, turned down the initial offer because he preferred The Saint. He was the oldest actor to take on 007 at 46 and also the oldest to leave it at 58; excluding Never Say Never Again (1983), only Daniel Craig spent longer in the role.

Daniel Craig, ranked third, entered facing skepticism for being too blond, lacking charisma, and too heavily built. After a superb debut in Casino Royale he won over audiences with Skyfall among his finest films, closing Bond's story with his death in No Time to Die.

Sean Connery, ranked second, created the character so completely that Fleming altered later novels to match him; his macho, violent, sophisticated and self-confident Bond established virtually every defining element of the cinematic formula. He also became a superb dramatic actor afterward.

Timothy Dalton, ranked first, came closest to Fleming's Bond and insisted on shaping scripts accordingly, turning down the role more times than anyone before accepting it in 1986—first feeling too young (before Lazenby was cast), then again in the mid-1980s. He played Bond in two outstanding films, The Living Daylights and Licence to Kill, declining a third after legal disputes left him waiting five years; by then he felt too old.

Looking ahead, Robert Pattinson will bring strong acting credentials and box-office appeal, chosen by director Denis Villeneuve—who had worked with him on Dune (screenplay by Steven Knight)—and producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman of Amazon Studios. For Amazon he is the safest choice assuming he never again plays the Dark Knight after The Batman Part II; he signed three films for continuity though he is already 40 years old, whereas rivals Jack Lowden, Callum Turner, Josh O'Connor and Nicholas Hoult are all 36.

Pattinson took Craig's physical territory into thoroughly physical ground—something not natural to him despite getting in shape for The Batman. James Hibberd of The Hollywood Reporter notes his angular quality often has a nervous or uncomfortable feel that makes him watchable, yet even romantic roles lean toward quirkiness; Pattinson is the first actor cast as Bond who seems more suited to play a villain than the hero.

Ian Fleming's 12 novels depicted a Scottish Royal Navy commander with dark hair and blue-grey eyes, standing 1.89 metres tall and weighing 93 kilos—lean rather than muscular, cold and calculating yet a bon vivant and gentleman, sophisticated but violent, resembling U.S. composer Hoagy Carmichael.

For screen-rights holders half-siblings Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson, the cinematic 007 must have presence, charm, personality and acting ability. When asked if Bond could be played by a woman, Broccoli told EL PAÍS: "No," it will always be a male character because Fleming wrote it that way; female protagonists should exist in their own right rather than transforming existing male characters.

The article's ranking is explicitly subjective and contested, with the worst-to-best order reflecting editorial judgment rather than objective measurement.
items.title: Ranking of James Bond actors from worst to best and Robert Pattinson's upcoming tenure as 007

items.summary: A new analysis of federal data by the think tank Energy Innovation indicates that U.S. electricity-sector carbon dioxide emissions are set to decline this year, even as demand remains record-high and the Trump administration works to sustain uncompetitive coal plants. Power plants burned 10% less coal through July 2026, a drop that drove power sector emissions down in the first half of 2026 and puts the U.S. on track for an overall energy-related emissions reduction of about 2% across the full year. This represents a reversal from 2025, when coal generation rose 13% and economy-wide emissions jumped 2.4%, driven by surging electricity demand combined with unusually high natural gas prices that made coal more economically attractive; in contrast, analysts attribute this year's decline to coal plants simply running less often — averaging 46.7% of the time through August 2026 versus 49.7% over the same period last year. The analysis suggests last year's coal resurgence was a temporary blip rather than the start of a sustained boom, despite continued soaring electricity demand. Coal's decline is notable given aggressive White House efforts to boost the fuel: the Department of Energy has ordered plants to stay open past planned retirement dates citing an alleged energy crisis — orders that have burdened consumers with hundreds of millions of dollars in costs even for some run-down facilities unable to produce power — while also announcing hundreds of millions of dollars in funding, and the Environmental Protection Agency has rolled back pollution regulations. Around 48 gigawatts of coal capacity shuttered during Trump's first term, more than either of Barack Obama's terms; last year saw only a small amount of retirements, so the fleet shrank by just 1.6% to about 167.5 GW as reported by Robbie Orvis, Energy Innovation's senior director of modeling and analysis. However, the report notes that old plants remaining online does not mean they contribute more; combined-cycle gas turbines did not pick up the slack, running at a slightly lower rate than last year through August, though overall gas consumption ticked up 3.8%, reflecting greater output from other facility types such as peaker plants. Meanwhile, new solar capacity has surged onto the grid with large-scale solar generation projected to rise 21% this year per federal data; in May, for the first month ever, solar outproduced coal on the U.S. grid according to think tank Ember; and batteries have continued displacing gas during high-value evening peak hours in California, Texas, and other markets. The report concludes that when coal use declines while gas stays roughly steady and renewables grow quickly, emissions fall as expected this year.
items.title: US power sector emissions projected to fall in 2026 amid lower coal use

items.summary: A new US recycling company called Jupiter has been formed by merging Solarcycle, a solar panel recycler, with PedalPoint Recycling, which is Korea Zinc's US recycling and metals business. The combined entity will send recovered silver and copper from retired solar panels and data center hardware to Korea Zinc refineries, including a $7.4 billion plant planned for Clarksville, Tennessee. Jupiter states it launches with eight certified US facilities, nearly 1 million square feet of processing space, and about 250 employees, while taking on customers from both predecessor businesses, including Microsoft, Prologis, and Brookfield. For solar farm or data center operators, the integration allows a single company to remove equipment from service, resell parts with remaining useful life, and recycle the remainder; customers can track where materials go and bring them back into their own supply chains. Korea Zinc will hold a majority stake in Jupiter. Solarcycle's Suvi Sharma is set to lead as CEO, while PedalPoint's Kevin Hahm serves as CFO. Microsoft and Prologis Ventures are among Solarcycle's existing investors. Regarding capacity, Solarcycle reported that its Cedartown, Georgia plant was processing thousands of old solar panels a week at opening and could handle up to 5 gigawatts' worth of panels annually at full capacity, recovering glass, aluminum, copper, and silver. The Tennessee facility adds a US refining step under Project Crucible, developed with US government backing and expected to start production in phases in 2029; the plant is designed to process about 1.1 million tons of raw materials per year and produce roughly 540,000 tons of finished products. The article also contains an unrelated promotional segment for EnergySage solar installer matching services, which offers no additional factual content on Jupiter or Korea Zinc.
items.title: Solarcycle and PedalPoint Recycling merge into Jupiter to supply Korea Zinc's $7.4B Tennessee refinery

items.summary: Arpan, a Mumbai-based non-profit dedicated to eliminating child sexual abuse in India and described as the country's largest NGO in this space with over 150 professionals, launched its eighth edition of Child Safety Week on November 14, running through November 20. The campaign carries the message 'Ruk Jao Varna POCSO Pakad Lega' ('Stop, or POCSO will catch you'), directed at those who sexually abuse children and aimed to counter what it calls the most dangerous phrase in child protection: chalta hai (No Big deal). Arpan frames six acts offenders often pass off as harmless—touching a child with sexual intent, looking at a child with sexual intent, taking sexual photos or videos of a child, asking a child for inappropriate photos or videos, showing a child sexual content, and viewing, saving or sharing child sexual abuse and exploitation material—and states each is punishable under the POCSO Act. The campaign argues that minimisation gives abusers permission while normalisation hides these behaviours in plain sight; it cites examples such as an uncle insisting a girl sit on his lap at every visit, an older cousin showing sexually explicit pictures framed as 'helping you grow up,' a stranger befriending a child online and coercing intimate photos, and someone forwarding a video of a child being sexually harassed with a laughing emoji. Arpan asserts that each excuse makes the next act easier and that these same excuses are later turned on children to keep them silent and used by others to dodge blame. Citing 2024 data, Arpan reports about 189 cases of sexual offences against children were registered under POCSO across India every day—nearly eight per hour—and notes these represent only the cases that reached a police station, with many more never reported. In 2024 penetrative sexual assault cases under POCSO, Arpan states 96.6 per cent of accused were known to the child, arguing familiarity and trust give abusers access while minimisation gives them permission. The campaign maintains none of these acts stops being a crime because it was called a game, joke or affection, since the law asks what someone did rather than whether they are family, meant it, or whether it happened on a screen; Arpan's closing line is 'nahi, nahi chalta hai.' About Arpan: founded in 2007 and based in Mumbai, it describes itself as globally recognised and award-winning, offering prevention and intervention (healing) services for children and adults, with over 150 professionals and more than 2 crore individuals impacted since 2007. The article notes the campaign's message is addressed to abusers rather than providing a broader public audience or detailing specific outcomes of Child Safety Week beyond its dates and edition number.
items.title: Arpan's Child Safety Week 2026 Warns Against Six Minimised Acts of Child Sexual Abuse Under POCSO

items.summary: Iran-backed Houthi forces have gained greater control over the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, a narrow waterway between Eritrea, Djibouti and Yemen that connects the Indian Ocean to the Red Sea and Suez Canal. The strait has already been closed or reduced to a bottleneck since September 2026 as part of broader regional conflict involving Iran, Ethiopia and Eritrea, forcing many cargo ships to be delayed or rerouted while businesses pass higher transport and fuel costs onto customers. This strategic and commercial importance has overshadowed the strait's role as a humanitarian corridor: it remains one of the world's most dangerous migration passages, where people cross on derelict boats with smugglers outside United Nations and governmental controls. Last year more than 900 people died or went missing trying to cross; in October 2026 a boat capsized off Djibouti carrying nearly 300 people escaping violence and persecution. Between January and August 2026, the U.N.'s International Organization for Migration recorded 122,258 arrivals to Yemen from the Horn of Africa — more than had crossed by that time in 2025 — with most migrants coming from Ethiopia and traveling without passports or visas. Since August, worsening displacement and insecurity have made accurate figures impossible to estimate. The strait is also a lifeline for commercial goods imported into Ethiopia, Kenya, Somaliland and Somalia; its disruption has compounded the effects of increased violence and displacement. Djibouti foreign minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar expressed grave concern before the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 26, 2026 about an influx of Yemeni refugees straining underresourced coastal towns and camps, while UNHCR reports a cholera outbreak in the Markazi refugee camp housing thousands of Yemenis who fled into northern Djibouti. Humanitarian aid transit has been similarly undermined by security risks, shipping delays and rising food and fuel costs: UNICEF's August 2026 situation report estimates nearly 5 million people in Somalia need urgent assistance, at least another 5.5 million in Ethiopia face needs from conflict combined with below-average rainfall linked to El Niño, and in Yemen an estimated 321,000 have been displaced since Aug. 1, 2026 while ongoing water scarcity leaves 17 million people without clean water, sanitation and hygiene services. The authors of the forthcoming book 'Refugees Without Refuge' argue that protecting safe movement of people and goods through the strait is key to averting future tragedies.
items.title: Houthi Control of Bab el-Mandeb Heightens Danger to Trade and Migration

items.summary: Moreangels Mbizah, a conservation biologist and founder of the nonprofit Wildlife Conservation Action (WCA), describes her work reducing human-wildlife conflict between African lions and communities in Zimbabwe. The organization began six years ago in two wards of Nyaminyami rural district; over five years it recorded a 98% reduction in conflict incidents there, while across Mbire and Binga districts conflict has fallen by 53%. WCA's approach centers on its 'community guardian' model—known as Batabilili—which trains young men and women from the communities to act as boots on the ground for mitigation. Guardians monitor lion movement, help farmers secure livestock in above-ground kraals, respond to incidents with tailored advice, hold community meetings, and provide emotional or psychological support after losses occur. Mbizah notes that a key driver of conflict was communities feeling unheard and unsupported; she says WCA's presence addresses this directly. The model has also reduced retaliatory killings of lions as attitudes shift from negative toward coexistence. Beyond mitigation, WCA is pursuing nature-based livelihood solutions such as beekeeping to increase community benefits while protecting forests at the edges of protected areas, which also deters elephants from crop fields. Outreach reaches over 30,000 people through school environmental clubs and seminars; Mbizah estimates around 40,000 people have received non-lethal mitigation approaches. She has mentored 432 female university students through the Conservation Sisters program, which pairs them with established mentors and offers one-year fellowships to recent graduates—inspired by her own experience as a Black Zimbabwean woman in conservation roughly two decades ago. WCA works closely with Zimparks (the Wildlife Management Authority) and the Ministry of Environment, Climate and Wildlife, and is developing a national human-wildlife conflict strategy following a July workshop. The organization uses GPS collars on lions and elephants for movement tracking and early warning, plus camera trapping to understand species distribution; it also shares data with authorities. WCA has expanded from two wards in Nyaminyami District to 10 wards there, then into Mbire, Binga, and now Hwange Districts along the Zambezi Valley across three transfrontier conservation areas linking Zimbabwe with Botswana and Kenya. Other organizations within Zimbabwe as well as abroad are adopting and adapting the model. Mbizah acknowledges WCA may not scale at its own desired rate but is scaling the idea through partnerships, and she sees lessons for Europe's rising wolf populations—though contexts differ, since lions have long coexisted with African communities while wolves were recently reintroduced there.
items.title: Zimbabwe NGO cuts lion–livestock conflict via community guardians
